subtopic_detail: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy
stem:
A 63 year old woman is referred to you with eight months of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels six to nine times daily including twice most nights. She has lost 3 kg. She has coeliac serology that is negative on a gluten containing diet, and normal thyroid function.

She takes pantoprazole started 14 months ago and sertraline. Faecal calprotectin is mildly raised, and stool cultures and parasite testing are negative. Colonoscopy was performed by a colleague and reported normal mucosa throughout to the terminal ileum, with random biopsies taken. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no mass and no tenderness.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), albumin 37 g/L (35-50), C-reactive protein within normal limits, faecal calprotectin 96 micrograms/g (less than 50), tissue transglutaminase antibody negative with normal immunoglobulin A

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.text: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea predominance triggered by her antidepressant
options.rationale: Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are alarm features that place this outside a functional diagnosis, which requires the absence of such features. Serotonergic drugs can loosen stools but would not produce eight months of nocturnal symptoms with weight loss. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.text: Microscopic colitis, in which inflammation is visible only on histological examination
options.rationale: Chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea including at night in an older woman with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy is the defining presentation, and the diagnosis rests entirely on the random biopsies that were taken. Proton pump inhibitors and serotonergic agents are both recognised precipitants. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.text: Bile acid diarrhoea following occult terminal ileal disease or previous cholecystectomy
options.rationale: Bile acid malabsorption typically follows ileal resection, ileal Crohn disease or cholecystectomy, and her terminal ileum was visualised and normal with no surgical history. It remains a differential that is tested by a trial of a bile acid sequestrant if histology is normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.text: Early Crohn disease with patchy inflammation not yet visible at colonoscopic examination
options.rationale: Crohn disease produces macroscopically visible aphthous ulceration or strictures and usually a substantially higher calprotectin with raised inflammatory markers. The near-pair distinction is that both raise calprotectin, but only microscopic colitis leaves the mucosa looking entirely normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Microscopic Colitis)

options.text: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth secondary to prolonged acid suppression therapy
options.rationale: Bacterial overgrowth characteristically causes bloating, flatulence and steatorrhoea rather than large volume watery nocturnal stools, and it does not raise faecal calprotectin. It would be tested by breath testing if the histology returned normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a common and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery diarrhoea, particularly in women over 50, and it accounts for a substantial minority of patients investigated for non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal endoscopic appearance. It comprises two histological subtypes, collagenous colitis with a thickened subepithelial collagen band and lymphocytic colitis with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, which behave similarly and are managed identically. Because the mucosa looks normal, the diagnosis is missed entirely unless random biopsies are taken from both the right and left colon during the procedure. Several drugs are implicated, most consistently proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and ranitidine, and withdrawal of the offending agent alone can produce remission. Where symptoms persist, budesonide is the treatment with the strongest evidence for inducing and maintaining remission, and there is an association with coeliac disease and other autoimmune conditions.
key_points: Suspect it in chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal colonoscopy in an older woman
Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are alarm features that exclude a functional diagnosis
Diagnosis requires random biopsies from right and left colon, since the mucosa appears normal
Proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and serotonergic agents are recognised triggers
Budesonide has the strongest evidence for inducing remission when drug withdrawal fails
explanation.pearls: Screen every patient for coeliac disease, because it coexists in a substantial minority and its presence changes management entirely; then stop the implicated drug before committing to budesonide, since withdrawal alone can resolve symptoms.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

subtopic_detail: Non-immune rubella serology identified on booking bloods
stem:
You are reviewing a 29 year old woman at 12 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her booking bloods. Her rubella IgG is reported as non-immune, although her childhood record documents two doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.

She feels well, has had no rash or fever, and has had no known contact with anyone with a rash illness. She works in an accounting office with no contact with young children. Her hepatitis B surface antigen, syphilis and HIV serology are negative, she is varicella immune, and her blood group is O positive. She asks whether she can simply have the vaccine now to protect the pregnancy.

data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG non-immune; varicella IgG immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; syphilis and HIV serology negative; blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the vaccine now, since the risk from a live vaccine in pregnancy is only theoretical
options.rationale: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, and although inadvertent administration has not been shown to cause congenital rubella syndrome, deliberate administration is not acceptable when the dose can safely be given after birth. Inadvertent exposure is managed with reassurance rather than termination. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the vaccine now and advise her to avoid pregnancy for the next 28 days
options.rationale: The 28 day rule applies to a woman who is not yet pregnant, and it cannot be applied to someone already 12 weeks pregnant. Applying the interval here reveals a misreading of when the precaution operates. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer vaccination and give it after birth before she leaves the maternity unit
options.rationale: The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but should be given in the immediate postpartum period, which is the reliable opportunity to protect future pregnancies, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication. In the meantime she is advised to avoid contact with anyone who has a rash illness and to present early if exposed. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give normal human immunoglobulin now to provide passive protection during pregnancy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin does not reliably prevent infection or congenital rubella syndrome and is not recommended as routine prophylaxis for a non-immune pregnant woman. Its limited role is after a significant confirmed exposure where termination would not be considered. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Repeat the antibody test at 28 weeks and vaccinate only if she remains non-immune
options.rationale: Repeat testing will not change management because vaccination remains contraindicated throughout pregnancy regardless of the result. Serial testing is used to detect seroconversion after a documented exposure, not to decide on routine vaccination. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaccination in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Rubella serology is checked at every antenatal booking not to protect the current pregnancy, which cannot be vaccinated, but to identify women who need immunisation afterwards so that future pregnancies are protected. Congenital rubella syndrome causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects and intellectual disability, with the risk of severe defects highest when infection occurs before 12 weeks and falling substantially after 16 weeks. A non-immune result despite documented vaccination is common, reflecting waning of measurable antibody rather than absent protection, but management follows the serology. The vaccine is live attenuated and therefore contraindicated in pregnancy, so the dose is given in the immediate postpartum period before discharge, where uptake is highest, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication. Women who are not yet pregnant are advised to avoid conception for 28 days after the dose, and inadvertent vaccination in early pregnancy is managed with reassurance because no case of congenital rubella syndrome has been attributed to the vaccine.
key_points: Booking serology identifies women for postpartum vaccination, not for treatment in this pregnancy
The vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated during pregnancy
Give the dose before discharge after birth, when uptake is highest; breastfeeding is not a contraindication
The 28 day conception interval applies only to women who are not currently pregnant
Risk of severe congenital defects is highest with infection before 12 weeks
explanation.pearls: Advise a non-immune pregnant woman to present immediately if she is exposed to a rash illness, because diagnosis of maternal rubella depends on paired serology and IgM taken close to the exposure rather than on the booking result.

subtopic_detail: Vaccination advice at a routine second trimester antenatal visit
stem:
You are reviewing a 31 year old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy at a routine antenatal visit. She received an influenza vaccine at 12 weeks in this pregnancy and has no allergies.

During her first pregnancy three years ago she was given a whooping cough vaccine at 30 weeks, and she asks whether she needs it again so soon. Her three year old is fully immunised on schedule. She has had no contact with anyone with a prolonged cough and feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on examination.

data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with iodine; influenza vaccine given at 12 weeks this pregnancy; diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine given at 30 weeks of her previous pregnancy three years ago

lead_in: What should you advise about whooping cough vaccination?

options.text: Give a diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine during this pregnancy now
options.rationale: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy irrespective of the interval since the last one, because maternal antibody wanes and it is transplacental transfer in this pregnancy that protects this newborn. The optimal window of 20 to 32 weeks allows time for antibody transfer before birth. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer vaccination until after the birth and vaccinate her and household contacts then
options.rationale: Vaccinating around the birth relies on reducing transmission from contacts rather than protecting the infant directly, and gives no transplacental antibody. This cocooning approach is the fallback for women who were not vaccinated during pregnancy. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Advise that no further dose is needed because she was vaccinated three years ago
options.rationale: Antibody from a previous pregnancy has waned and does not cross the placenta in this one, so a prior dose does not protect this baby. The minimum interval concern that applies to other tetanus containing vaccines does not override the recommendation in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer the dose until 36 weeks so that her antibody levels peak closer to the birth
options.rationale: Vaccinating late leaves insufficient time for antibody production and placental transfer, and offers no protection at all to a baby born preterm. Doses after 32 weeks are still given if the opportunity was missed, but they are second best. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaccination in Pregnancy)

options.text: Check her pertussis serology and vaccinate only if her antibody titres are found low
options.rationale: Serology is not recommended for this purpose because no protective antibody threshold is established and results would not change the recommendation to vaccinate. Testing would only delay a vaccine that is indicated regardless of the result. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Pertussis causes its most severe disease in infants under six months, who are too young to have completed their own primary course, and the majority of infant deaths occur before the first scheduled dose at six weeks. Maternal vaccination works by generating antibody that crosses the placenta, and it is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of how recently a previous dose was given, because transfer only benefits the infant of the pregnancy in which the vaccine was administered. The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, which allows time for the maternal antibody response and for active placental transfer, and vaccination in this window prevents the large majority of infant cases. Doses given after 32 weeks are still worthwhile but produce lower infant antibody levels, and vaccination before 20 weeks may result in waning before birth. Influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of pregnancy, and both vaccines are safe and funded, with the wider household encouraged to be up to date as an additional layer.
key_points: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of the interval since the last
The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks to allow antibody production and placental transfer
Protection works through transplacental antibody, so it is pregnancy specific
Infants are most vulnerable before their first scheduled dose at six weeks
Serological testing has no role because no protective threshold is defined
explanation.pearls: Vaccinating in the 20 to 32 week window rather than at 36 weeks matters most for babies born preterm, who otherwise arrive before any meaningful transplacental antibody has been transferred.

subtopic_detail: Fever and a discharging abdominal wound six days after caesarean section
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman who presents six days after an emergency caesarean performed at full dilatation. She reports two days of increasing pain at the wound with fever and a discharge that has stained her dressing.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she had gestational diabetes managed with insulin. On examination the lower transverse wound has erythema extending 4 cm beyond the incision line with surrounding induration, and serous fluid discharges from the lateral third when gentle pressure is applied. The uterus is non-tender, lochia is not offensive, and there is no calf tenderness or leg swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.3 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Open and drain the infected wound segment and commence intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A collection under an infected wound will not resolve on antibiotics alone, so the discharging portion is opened along its length to drain and allow healing by secondary intention, with a swab taken at the same time to guide therapy. Her fever, tachycardia and inflammatory response justify the intravenous route rather than oral treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

options.text: Prescribe oral cephalexin and arrange community nurse review of the wound in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy without drainage leaves the collection in place and understates a systemic inflammatory response with fever and tachycardia. This approach suits mild cellulitis around an intact wound in a well patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT abdomen and pelvis before any antimicrobial treatment is commenced
options.rationale: The infection is clinically evident at the wound and imaging would delay both drainage and antibiotics without changing the immediate plan. Cross sectional imaging is indicated when a deep pelvic collection or uterine dehiscence is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for endometritis and observe the wound expectantly
options.rationale: Endometritis produces a tender uterus with offensive lochia, both of which are absent, so treating the wrong site leaves the wound collection undrained. The two complications can coexist, which is why both are examined for explicitly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for immediate return to theatre for full wound resuture under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Primary closure of an infected wound traps bacteria and leads to breakdown, so these wounds are managed open with secondary healing or delayed closure. Theatre is required when there is fascial dehiscence or suspected necrotising infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

explanation.summary: Surgical site infection complicates a meaningful proportion of caesarean births and is the most common cause of readmission afterwards, with raised body mass index, diabetes, prolonged labour, emergency surgery at full dilatation and prolonged rupture of membranes all increasing risk. Infection typically declares itself between days four and eight, after discharge from hospital, so the presentation is usually to a general practice or emergency department rather than the maternity ward. The essential principle is that antibiotics alone do not treat a collection, so an infected wound with fluctuance or discharge is opened and drained, swabbed, and then managed open with dressings to heal by secondary intention. Assessment must also distinguish and exclude endometritis, deep pelvic collection, venous thromboembolism and, rarely, necrotising soft tissue infection, since pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapidly spreading discolouration demands immediate surgical review. Prevention is largely achieved through prophylactic antibiotics given before the skin incision rather than after cord clamping, along with skin preparation and glycaemic control.
key_points: Infection usually appears between days four and eight, after hospital discharge
Raised body mass index, diabetes and emergency surgery at full dilatation raise the risk
Antibiotics alone will not resolve a collection; the wound must be opened and drained
Endometritis is distinguished by a tender uterus and offensive lochia
Pain out of proportion with rapidly spreading change suggests necrotising infection
explanation.pearls: Prophylactic antibiotics given within the 60 minutes before skin incision, rather than after cord clamping, roughly halve the rate of maternal infection without adverse neonatal effects, and this timing is now standard Australian practice.

subtopic_detail: Maternal exposure to a childhood exanthem and surveillance for foetal anaemia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 33 year old childcare worker at 15 weeks in her second pregnancy. Ten days ago several children in her room developed a bright red facial rash followed by a lace-like rash on their limbs, and one was diagnosed by a general practitioner.

She has had mild joint aches in both hands for three days but no rash and no fever. Her booking bloods showed rubella immunity and negative syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV serology. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Examination reveals no rash, no lymphadenopathy and a uterus consistent with dates. Urgent serology now returns parvovirus B19 IgM positive with IgG negative.

data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; rubella IgG immune; full blood count within normal limits; ultrasound today shows a single live foetus with normal anatomy, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the high risk of severe congenital malformation
options.rationale: This infection does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome, and the risk is transient foetal anaemia rather than structural anomaly, so this advice is factually wrong and would cause avoidable harm. Structural teratogenesis is the concern with rubella, not with this virus. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

options.text: Reassure her that the normal scan today excludes any risk to the foetus from this infection
options.rationale: Anaemia and hydrops typically develop two to six weeks after maternal infection, so a normal scan at 10 days provides no reassurance about the weeks that follow. A single normal scan is adequate only once the surveillance window has passed. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

options.text: Commence maternal intravenous immunoglobulin to prevent transplacental viral transmission
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no established role in preventing transmission or treating foetal infection with this virus, and no antiviral therapy exists. Treatment is directed at the consequence, foetal anaemia, rather than at the virus. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction to confirm foetal infection
options.rationale: Confirming foetal infection does not change management because surveillance and intervention are driven by evidence of anaemia rather than by the presence of viral genome. The procedure adds a miscarriage risk without altering the plan. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler for the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: The serology confirms recent maternal infection, and the risk to the foetus is aplastic anaemia leading to hydrops during a window of roughly two to 12 weeks afterwards, detected non-invasively by a rising peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery. Detecting anaemia before hydrops allows intrauterine transfusion, which is the intervention that saves these pregnancies. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy matters because the virus targets erythroid precursors, and the short foetal red cell lifespan combined with rapid expansion of red cell mass makes the foetus vulnerable to profound aplastic anaemia. Around half of adults are already immune, and IgG positivity with negative IgM indicates past infection and no risk. The virus is not teratogenic, so structural anomaly is not the concern; instead the risks are foetal anaemia, hydrops and loss, and these are greatest when infection occurs before 20 weeks. The interval from maternal infection to hydrops is typically two to six weeks and can extend to 12, which defines the surveillance period. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median identifies significant anaemia non-invasively and triggers referral for intrauterine transfusion, after which survival is good and long term outcomes for survivors are generally normal.
key_points: The virus causes foetal anaemia by suppressing erythroid precursors, not congenital malformation
IgG positive with IgM negative indicates past infection and immunity, requiring no action
Hydrops develops two to 12 weeks after maternal infection, so one normal scan is insufficient
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity detects anaemia non-invasively before hydrops appears
Intrauterine transfusion is the treatment and carries good survival when performed in time
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median is the trigger for referral for intrauterine transfusion, and it detects anaemia well before ascites or pericardial effusion appear on the scan.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections
